Words in this topic (19)
App
A program someone uses, the thing with buttons. It is the app that talks to the model. The model itself has no interface, no memory and no idea that a person exists.
API
A way for one program to ask another program to do something, over the internet. You never see it. When this book says your app "calls the API", it means your app sent a message to the model provider’s computers and waited for a reply.
JSON
A plain-text way of writing structured information so a program can read it: labels and values inside curly braces, like {"role": "user", "content": "hello"}. It is a data format, not code or a database. API requests and responses are written in it.
Endpoint
The specific web address a program sends its request to. Different endpoints do different jobs — one for chat, one for embeddings.
Payload
Whatever is inside the request or reply. The contents of the envelope, as opposed to the envelope itself.
Parameter
A setting you pass with a request — temperature, maximum length, which model. Confusingly, the same word also means the billions of internal numbers a model was trained with. In this book it means the setting unless it says otherwise.
Notebook
A web page where you can type a few lines of code, press a button, and see what happens underneath. It is the tool this book uses so you never have to install anything. Nothing you do in one can break anything.
Runtime
The machine actually running your code. In this app it is Python inside your browser tab, so a reload starts a fresh one, and Restore puts your definitions back. A hosted notebook such as Colab lends you a machine for a few hours and then takes it back.
Deploy
To put a change where real users can reach it. Until something is deployed it exists only on your machine.
Rollback
Putting the previous version back after a bad deploy. It undoes your code. It does not undo a model’s behaviour, which is why Chapter 18 insists a kill switch is a different thing.
Corpus
All the documents your system is allowed to answer from, taken together. Your set of source material. Plural: corpora.
Index
A prepared copy of your corpus, arranged so searching it is fast. Building one is called indexing. Nothing can be retrieved until it has been indexed.
Pipeline
A sequence of steps where each one’s output is the next one’s input. Documents in at one end, an answer out at the other. Chapter 7 draws yours.
Latency
How long the user waits. Measured in seconds, and a product decision rather than a technical detail.
p95
The wait that 95 out of 100 people get or better — so it describes the slow fifth of your users rather than the typical one. Averages hide these people; p95 is what you design for.
SLA
Service-level agreement. A supplier’s written promise about uptime or speed, with a consequence attached if they break it. A promise without a consequence is a marketing claim, not an SLA.
Deterministic
Same input, same output, every time. Ordinary software is deterministic. A language model is not, which is the source of most of the surprise in this field.
Orchestration
Coordinating several steps or several models so they run in the right order and hand results to each other.
Taxonomy
A named set of categories. In Chapter 14 it means your list of the ways your system fails, in your own words, with a count against each.
1Product foundations: the problem, the people and the plan✓

Before any code, you do a product manager’s first work. You name a problem, talk to the people who have it, size the market, choose what to do first and write it down. Month 1 needs nothing installed.

Builds on

Before you start

Read in the book

  1. Book 1 The Number in the Chat ~11 minA product manager finds identity numbers in a week of customer chats and has to decide whether the finding deserves a year of work. Along the way you learn about personal data, counting before deciding, choosing between problems, and writing a decision down.
  2. Book 2 Four Questions Before Building ~9 minAn engineer tests a promising idea against the four ways products fail, using a feature that nobody found as the example. You learn the three stages of making a product, the four product risks, and the difference between selling to people and selling to companies.
  3. Book 3 Asking About Yesterday ~10 minA first conversation with a colleague produces only agreement, and five better ones produce evidence. You learn how to question people about their past, how to read what they were trying to achieve, and how to find the one assumption to test first.
  4. Book 4 Who Else Is Standing Here ~10 minA conditional yes from the compliance head sets one hard requirement for the tool, and the product manager then checks what already exists, sizes the market from the bottom up, and studies the competition, including the competitor that is not a product.
  5. Book 5 Choosing What Not to Do ~8 minA list of nine good ideas is not a strategy. A retired teacher's question leads the product manager to write one. She chooses a narrow first target and a single measure of success, names the product, and ranks the work with scores that she is willing to overrule.
  6. Book 6 A Plan Others Can Believe ~10 minA strategy is a sentence until other people can act on it. You learn to promise outcomes instead of dates, to write goals as measurable results, to map who can say no, and to imagine the project has already failed.
  7. Book 7 Writing It Down So Others Can Build It ~10 minAn engineer sketches the guard on a napkin and the product manager turns the sketch into a specification that a stranger could build from. You learn the four parts of the guard, requirements and acceptance criteria, thin first versions, and what a paper test shows that a meeting cannot.
  8. Book 8 What the Machine Is ~12 minA product manager who has said "powered by AI" for two years tries to explain what it means and cannot. We build the answer from the ground up: language models, tokens, the context window, attention, how a model is made and used, and the two kinds of AI.

Your project

Project stage 1 Decide what you are building, and why

Before any code, you do the work a product manager does first. You name the problem and study the existing tool. You talk to real people, size the market and choose a strategy. Then you plan the work and write the requirements. You also run first experiments to see how AI models behave on Indian text.

Words in this topic (39)
Artifact
Something you made that another person can open and check: a document, a spreadsheet, a notebook, a prototype or a dashboard. In this book, progress is measured in artifacts, not in pages read.
Mastery gate
The check at the end of every chapter. Score each artifact 0–3. Move on only when all score at least 2 and no safety, privacy or evidence item scores 0.
Decision log
A running file where you record each decision with its date, the evidence behind it, and what would make you change it.
Repository
A folder on a site such as GitHub that keeps a project’s files and every earlier version of them, with a note on each change.
Commit
One saved version of the files in a repository, with a short message saying what changed.
Formula
A cell in a spreadsheet that starts with = and works out its value from other cells, so it changes when they change.
B2B / B2C
Business-to-business and business-to-consumer. In B2B you sell to companies, and the people who pay, use and approve the product are often different people. In B2C you sell to individuals, who usually pay and use it themselves.
Product sense
The habit of checking an idea against four risks before building it. Will people want it (value)? Can they use it (usability)? Can we build it (feasibility)? Does it work for the business (viability)?
Jobs to be done
The idea that people “hire” a product to make progress in a particular situation. Written as: “When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome].”
Leading question
An interview question that suggests the answer the interviewer wants, such as “Isn’t it frustrating when…?” People tend to agree, so the answer is weak evidence.
Persona
A short description of a type of user, their goals, workflow and pains. Useful only when every line traces back to real interviews.
Journey map
The steps a user goes through to get a job done, with what they do, think and feel at each step, and where the pain is.
Riskiest unknown
The assumption that would do the most damage if it were wrong and that you are least sure of. Test it first.
TAM / SAM / SOM
Three sizes of market. Total addressable market: everyone with the problem. Serviceable addressable market: the part you can actually serve. Serviceable obtainable market: what you could realistically win in a few years.
Positioning statement
One or two sentences saying who a product is for, what it does for them, and how it differs from the main alternative.
Moat
An advantage that is hard for competitors to copy, such as deep workflow integration, unique data or earned trust. A prompt or a newer model is not a moat.
Opportunity solution tree
A diagram with an outcome at the top, the user needs and pains from interviews below it, then possible solutions, then tests. It stops you jumping straight to a solution.
Wedge
The narrow first use case you can clearly win, chosen because it leads on to something bigger.
North Star metric
The one number that best measures the value customers get from a product, such as “issues caught in their first week”. Chapter B3 covers it in detail.
RICE
A prioritisation score: reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort. Useful for comparing options consistently, but only as good as the guesses you put in.
Cost of delay
What you lose for every week an item waits. High when there is a deadline, such as a contract renewal.
Outcome roadmap
A roadmap in three columns (now, next and later) where each item is an outcome to achieve rather than a feature with a date.
Kill criterion
A result, decided in advance, that means you stop working on something. For example: “stop if fewer than half of design partners act on an alert within four weeks”.
OKRs
Objectives and key results. The objective says what you want in words; the 3–4 key results are numbers that show you got there. Key results should be outcomes, not outputs.
Guardrail metric
A number that must not get worse while you chase a goal, such as false-alarm rate or cost per customer. It stops a team hitting a target in a way that harms users.
Stakeholder map
A grid of the people involved in a decision, placed by how much influence they have and how much they care. It shows who to work closely with and who can veto.
Pre-mortem
Before starting, imagine the project has failed and write down why. It surfaces risks people would not raise about a live plan.
PRD
Product requirements document: what to build, for whom and why, starting from the problem and its evidence. Chapter 18 covers the AI-specific version.
User story
One piece of value from the user’s point of view: “As a [role], I want [action], so that [benefit].” Each story needs acceptance criteria and edge cases.
MVP
Minimum viable product: the smallest thing that tests your riskiest assumption with real users. Not a small version of the whole product.
Vertical slice
A thin version of a feature that goes through every layer, from input to user value, so a real user can try it early.
Time-box
A fixed amount of time for uncertain work, with a result that counts as success and a plan if you do not reach it.
Usability test
Watching a real user try to complete a task with your product, without helping, to see where they get stuck.
Transformer
The model design behind today’s LLMs. It reads every token in the context at once and learns which earlier tokens matter for predicting the next one.
Inference
Running a trained model to get an answer. Training changes the model; inference only uses it. Most of your bill is inference.
Pre-training
The first, most expensive training stage: the model learns to predict the next token over a huge amount of text.
Instruction tuning
Training after pre-training on examples of instructions and good answers, so the model follows requests instead of just continuing text.
RLHF
Reinforcement learning from human feedback. People rank model answers, and the model is trained toward the answers they prefer.
Open-weight model
A model whose trained weights are published, so you can download and run it yourself instead of calling a vendor’s API.
2Meet the machine: tokens, your first call, memory and instructions✓

You meet a model on your own text. You learn to read a few lines of Python, connect a free model, send your first call and read its bill. Then you find out why it forgets, and how instructions change its answers.

Builds on

Nothing from an earlier topic.

Read in the book

  1. Book 9 The First Conversation ~8 minAn engineer shows the product manager a single request to a language model and the reply that comes back. The receipt attached to the reply turns out to teach as much as the answer. You learn about APIs, JSON, how to read a few lines of Python, API keys, the usage block, and why a confident answer is not evidence.
  2. Book 10 A Mind With No Memory ~7 minA language model keeps nothing from one request to the next. What looks like memory in a chatbot is the application sending the whole conversation again each time. This chapter shows how that works, what it costs, and why it makes the privacy problem at the centre of the project bigger.
  3. Book 11 Giving Instructions ~9 minThe team asks a language model to do the guard's work for the first time, and watches it fail in three different ways. This chapter explains prompts, system prompts, temperature, hallucination and worked examples. It also shows the difference between making a failure rarer and removing its cause.

  2. 0.8 Reading Python: just enough for this course ~25 min8 hands-on exercises
  3. 1 Your first API call: how a model answers ~45 min3 hands-on exercises · Project task: Make your first call and measure what it costs
  4. 1.5 Context windows and statelessness: why models forget ~25 min2 hands-on exercises · Project task: Work out what checking a long chat costs
  5. 2 System prompts, temperature and hallucination ~35 min3 hands-on exercises · Project task: Write the instructions for the AI helper, and try to break them
  6. 2.1 Writing prompts: four techniques that work ~25 min4 hands-on exercises · Project task: Improve the instructions until a stranger can use them
  7. Try Connect a model, once ~15 minDo the Connect page, one section at a time: get a free key, paste it in, and run the test call. You saw tokens and cost in Chapter 0.5, so you know what the key pays for. If a step fails, the page says why; copy the exact error into your notes.

Words in this topic (14)
Model / LLM
A prediction machine trained on huge amounts of text. It continues a piece of text in a way that sounds likely. It does not look things up.
API call
One question goes in, one answer comes out, and you get charged for it once. Your app sends a request to the model’s servers and waits for the reply.
Token
A small piece of a word. It is the unit a model reads, writes and bills in. One token is roughly ¾ of an English word.
Context window
The most text a model can handle in one request. It counts everything that goes in and everything that comes out, together. Think of it as the size of one envelope.
Stateless
The model remembers nothing between requests. Each request starts from a blank slate on the model’s side.
usage
The receipt for a request. It shows how many prompt tokens were read in and how many completion tokens were written out.
System prompt
A standing instruction that goes along with every message, out of the user’s sight. It tells the AI how to behave.
Temperature
A setting that decides whether the AI always picks its most likely next guess, or sometimes picks a less likely one. A low setting gives repeatable answers. It doesn’t make them true.
Hallucination
When the AI gives you something that sounds fluent but is made up, because it had no evidence to go on. This isn’t a malfunction. It is how a guessing machine normally behaves when it has nothing to go on.
Guardrail
Anything that reduces harmful or wrong outputs. The simplest kind is a single sentence in the system prompt.
Prompt
The text your app sends to the model — the user’s question plus any standing instructions attached to it. Mostly ordinary English, not a magic phrase.
Variable
A name that holds a value, so later lines of code can use it. In city = "Pune", the name city is the variable. Read the equals sign as “is now”.
Dictionary
In Python, pairs of a label and a value inside curly braces, like a small form: {"role": "user", "content": "hello"}. Every message to a model is written this way.
Few-shot
Putting two or three worked examples of the task inside the prompt, so the model copies their pattern. Zero-shot means asking with no examples at all.
3Testing it, and the first jobs: sorting and summarising✓

Before you trust a model, you build an answer key to check it against. Then you give it its first two jobs: sorting messages into groups, and summarising them.

Builds on

  • Four prompt techniques from 2.1, Topic 2 You have four versions of one prompt, and no way yet to choose between them.
  • A confident answer is not evidence from 2, Topic 2 Fluent text is not proof of a correct answer.
  • A prompt is a specification from 2.1, Topic 2 Four techniques shape what comes back.

Read in the book

  1. Book 12 Knowing Whether It Works ~8 minThe team stops trusting how an answer feels, and writes down the correct answers before looking at the tool's. This chapter covers test sets, answer keys, scoreboards, changing one thing at a time, and the five kinds of job a request can be.
  2. Book 13 Sorting and Summarising ~7 minOne job has a right answer and one does not. The team measures a sorter and finds a failure that a single score was hiding, then checks a summary for the facts it left out. This chapter introduces classifiers, the cost of each kind of error, and the must-keep list.

  4. 2.5 Summarisation: testing what a summary keeps ~25 min3 hands-on exercises · Project task: Write a short privacy report, and check it against the facts

4Finding things: cutting text, words and meaning✓

Long text has to be cut into pieces before a model can use it. Then you find the right piece two ways: by matching words, and by matching meaning.

Builds on

  • There is a size limit from 1, Topic 2 Everything sent in one call has to fit in the context window.
  • You pay for everything you send from 1, Topic 2 You pay per token, on every call.
  • Models invent answers when they have no evidence from 2, Topic 2 So the fix is to give them real evidence.

Words in this topic (17)
Chunk
One piece of a document after it has been cut up. It is the unit that gets stored, searched and sent to the model.
Chunking
The cutting itself. It looks like a boring chore, but it is a real design decision.
Fixed-size chunking
Cutting after every N words, whatever the text means.
Semantic chunking
Cutting at the places where the document’s own structure divides it.
Chunk overlap
Repeating the last lines of one chunk at the start of the next one. That way, an answer that sits across the boundary isn’t lost.
Retrieval
Fetching, from all the stored chunks, the few that are most likely to answer a question.
Keyword search
Finding text by the words it shares with the question. It matches spelling and is blind to meaning.
Query
The question that comes in.
Hybrid search
Running keyword search and semantic search together, then merging their results.
Top-k
Take only the best k results. The number k is a dial between recall and precision.
Embedding
The position a piece of text gets on the meaning map, written as a list of numbers. A small AI whose only job is placing text produces it.
Embedding model
The mapmaker. It reads text and gives back its address on the map.
Cosine similarity
A quick test of how close two pieces of text are. The higher the number, the closer they are in meaning.
Semantic search
Finding text by its address on the meaning map, instead of by its spelling.
query vs. passage
A label you give when you create an embedding, saying whether the text is a question or a piece of a document. If you skip it, quality drops quietly and nothing warns you.
Vector database
A system that stores embeddings and can quickly find the ones nearest to a given one.
Vector
A list of numbers. When this course says a piece of text has a “position” on the meaning map, the position is a vector — a few hundred numbers describing where it sits. You never look at them.

Words in this topic (7)
Evaluation
Grading your system against answers you have already checked. It is like acceptance testing, but for AI.
Ground truth
The answer key: a set of questions with verified correct answers, written before you test anything. Without one, “is it good?” has no answer.
Recall
Out of everything that mattered, how much did you fetch? Low recall means you missed files.
Precision
Out of everything you fetched, how much mattered? Low precision means a desk buried in paper.
Acceptance criteria
The numbers and behaviours you agree on in advance, which the system must meet before it goes live.
RAG
Retrieval-Augmented Generation. First you retrieve text that has been checked, then the model writes its answer from that text.
Rubric
A scoring guide written in advance: what each level of quality looks like, so two people grading the same thing agree.

Words in this topic (21)
Schema
A formal description of the shape an output must have: which fields it has, their types, and which are required.
Structured output
Model output that is held to a schema, instead of free-flowing prose.
Constrained decoding
At each step, the model is allowed to pick only tokens that fit the schema. That makes invalid output impossible, not just unlikely.
Enum
A field that can only hold a value from a fixed list.
Refusal path
What the product does when it should not answer. It gives a structured way to say “cannot determine” instead of inventing something. You design it on purpose, or it happens by accident.
Validation loop
Parse the output, validate it, and if it fails, ask again with the error attached.
Tool / function calling
You describe functions that can be called, so the model can ask for one to be run instead of answering in prose.
Agent loop
The model asks for a tool, your code runs it, the result goes back to the model, and this repeats.
Step budget
A hard limit on how many times the loop may run. It is not optional.
Trace
The recorded list of steps, calls, arguments and results for one run.
Side-effect boundary
The line between tools that only read and tools that change something in the world.
Context engineering
Deciding what goes into the envelope, in what order, and what gets pushed out. It is about the contents, not about how the prompt is worded.
Context rot
The model uses its context less well as the context grows, long before it hits the limit.
Lost in the middle
The model finds material at the start and the end far more reliably than material in the middle.
Prompt caching
The provider reuses the part at the start of a request that it has already processed. Put the stable parts first and the changing parts last.
Compaction
Summarising older context to free up budget, while keeping the most recent part word for word.
Reasoning model
A model that does some working-out of its own before it gives its answer.
Test-time compute
Paying for more accuracy on each query while the model runs, instead of paying for it during training.
Thinking budget
The setting that controls how much working-out the model is allowed. Setting it is a product decision.
p50 / p95 latency
The median response time, and the response time of the slow tail. Users feel the tail.
JSON schema
A written description of the exact shape a piece of JSON must have: which fields, of what type, and which are required. A program checks each answer against it.

Words in this topic (22)
BM25
A statistical way of ranking keyword matches that gives more weight to rare words. It is Chapter 4’s scoreboard, done properly.
Reciprocal rank fusion
A way to merge ranked lists by adding up 1/(rank) for each item. It is simple, sturdy and hard to beat.
Reranker
A model that scores a (question, chunk) pair by reading both together. You apply it only to a short list.
Contextual retrieval
Before embedding each chunk, you add a sentence, written by a model, that says where the chunk comes from. This fixes orphan chunks, the ones that make no sense on their own.
Query rewriting
Turning a half-sentence from a conversation into a complete question that can be searched on its own.
Metadata filter
Dropping chunks that are out of scope, such as the wrong version, date or department, before any scoring happens.
Prompt injection
Instructions slipped into a model’s input that change how it behaves.
Indirect injection
The attack comes inside content the system reads, such as a document, email, ticket or page.
Lethal trifecta
Private data, untrusted content and a way to communicate outside, all in one system. Any two of the three are safe.
Exfiltration
Getting private data out, for example through an email, a webhook, a URL parameter or a rendered image.
Confused deputy
A component with special privileges is tricked into using them for someone who has none.
Allowlist
A closed list of destinations that are allowed. It still protects you after an injection succeeds.
LLM-as-judge
Using a model to grade outputs against a rubric.
Judge agreement
How often the judge agrees with human labels. This number tells you whether the judge is usable.
Error analysis
Reading real outputs and sorting the failures into named groups as you go. It is the most useful single activity in the field.
Failure taxonomy
Your own named categories of failure, taken from your own traffic.
Regression suite
The cases that must pass before any release ships.
Offline vs online eval
Offline means testing against an answer key before release. Online means looking at what users get after release.
Drift
When behaviour changes over time without anyone changing the code — a model updated, a corpus grown, traffic shifted.
Pairwise comparison
Asking which of two answers is better, instead of scoring one answer out of ten. More reliable, because people and models are better at comparing than at grading.
Verbosity bias
A grader’s habit of scoring longer answers higher, even when they say nothing extra.
Position bias
A grader’s habit of preferring whichever answer it was shown first.

Words in this topic (15)
Cost per query
The full cost of one request the user can see, including retries and agent steps.
Cascade
Try the cheap model first, and move up to a bigger one if a check fails. It is the main pattern for controlling cost in production.
Model routing
Choosing a model for each request, based on how hard that request is.
Unit economics
The cost and revenue for each unit of use. This number decides whether a feature survives.
Vision-language model
A model that reads images and text together.
Page-as-chunk
Using a whole rendered page as the unit you retrieve, instead of a span of text.
Modality gap
Information that is on the page but missing from the text pulled out of it.
Turn detection
Deciding when a speaker has finished talking. It is the core problem of voice interfaces.
Blended rate
What you pay per query on average once traffic is spread across several models at different prices.
Cache hit rate
The share of your input that the provider recognised from a previous request and charged less for.
Vision model
A model that reads pictures as well as text — so you can hand it a page image instead of extracted text.
OCR
Software that turns a picture of a page into text. It keeps the words and throws away the layout.
Layout
Where things sit on a page — rows, columns, boxes. It carries meaning that plain text loses.
Barge-in
A person talking over the system mid-sentence. Voice interfaces have to handle it; text ones never face it.
DPDP Act
India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, with its Rules from 2025. It says what an organisation must do before it collects, uses or shares personal data, such as asking for consent.

Words in this topic (23)
Risk tier
How strict your obligations are. It depends on what happens if the system is wrong, not on the technology.
System card
A short document describing what an AI feature is for, what it was measured at, where it fails, and who checks it.
Data lineage
Where data came from, what right you have to use it, where it is kept, and for how long.
Human oversight
A defined point where a person can review the output, and has the authority to overrule it.
Shadow AI
Staff using AI tools that nobody approved. This really happens and can be measured. It isn’t a hypothetical.
AI PRD
A product specification where the acceptance criteria are eval thresholds, measured on a named dataset.
Model pinning
Fixing an exact model version, so the behaviour doesn’t change underneath you.
Deprecation migration
The re-evaluation you have to do when a provider retires the model you use.
Kill switch
A flag you can flip at once to send traffic to the path that doesn’t use AI. It is not a rollback.
Fine-tuning
Continuing a model’s training on your own examples so it adopts a behaviour. Teaches shape and register, not durable facts. Chapter 19 is the decision.
Audit trail
A record of what the system did and why, kept so someone can check it afterwards.
Data residency
Which country your data is physically stored and processed in.
Subprocessor
Another company your provider passes your data to. Their risk becomes yours.
Eval threshold
The number a release has to hit before it ships. An acceptance criterion with a figure in it.
Staged rollout
Releasing to a small slice of users first and watching the numbers before going wider.
Distillation
Training a small model to copy a large one on one narrow job. You get most of the quality at a fraction of the cost.
Portability
Whether an improvement survives changing providers. A better prompt and index travel with you; a tuned model does not.
Diagnosis
Naming which kind of wrong you have, with counts, before choosing what to change.
Interface contract
What the product promises to show at each level of certainty — and what it lets the user do about it.
Resolvable citation
A source link that opens the exact passage the claim came from, not just the name of a document.
Correction path
How a user fixes a wrong output, and what that fix records for you.
Graceful degradation
What the feature can still do when the AI part is switched off.
Governance
The rules, documents and named people that decide how an AI system may be used, who checks it, and who answers for it when it goes wrong.

How much work a system gets through in a given time, such as requests per minute. Latency is how long one request waits; throughput is how many get done.

You build the whole project, break it on purpose, measure it, ship it where people can use it, and defend your choices as you would in a review.

Read in the book

  1. Book 42 Who Pays, and How Much ~9 minA lender's technical lead asks what the guard would cost him. The answer turns on three different people, four ways of charging, and one row of a table that most price lists never draw. The chapter explains seat, usage, outcome and hybrid pricing, contribution margin, flywheels and gross margin.
  2. Book 43 How People Find It and Stay ~9 minA tool that nobody finds protects nobody. Five developers are handed a README and nothing else, a stopwatch records where they give up, and a spelling checker shows where the first moment of value has to happen. The chapter explains AARRR, activation, time-to-value, the Fogg behaviour model, product-led growth, growth loops, network effects, virality and dark patterns.
  3. Book 44 Counting What Matters ~9 minOnce real people use the tool, the question changes from "does it work?" to "what do they do?" A privacy product has to answer it without recording anything it exists to hide. A sample-size sum then shows why a young company can't run the test it wants. The chapter explains event taxonomies, tracking plans, cohorts, A/B tests and the minimum detectable effect.
  4. Book 45 The Tools and the Harness ~14 minA new engineer asks which tool is for what, and an experienced one answers with a drawing of slots, not a list of brands. The same engineer then builds a weekly report twice, once with fixed steps and once with an agent, and the two are measured on the same twenty weeks. The chapter explains toolchains, claim audits, the harness, project memory, allowlists, verifiers, sub-agents, state machines, feature flags, rollback triggers and incident reviews.
  5. Book 46 Real People, Real Use ~10 minA demonstration works while you are watching it. A product has to work when nobody is, for people who owe you nothing. In the spring Anaya prepares the guard for strangers, recruits them honestly, watches without helping, and ships one change because of what she saw. The chapter explains design partners, informed consent, observation sessions, changelogs and support logs.
  6. Book 47 The Work, and the Job ~11 minA former bank analyst has built something real and doesn't know how to show it. Over a few Sunday evenings Anaya helps her turn a year of work into a picture of the jobs she wants, a page of evidence, and a rehearsed way of answering the questions that decide whether she gets them. The chapter explains role matrices, case studies, product sense, system-design interviews, the STAR method and take-home assignments.

Words in this topic (26)
Willingness to pay
The most a buyer would spend to solve a problem. It is set by what their current alternative costs them, not by your costs.
Contribution margin
What each customer leaves you after the costs that grow with them, such as model calls and support. Usually shown as a percentage of revenue.
Gross margin
Revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the product. For AI products, the model vendor’s bill is a large part of that cost.
Flywheel
A loop where using the product makes it better, which brings more use. It can run on data, on workflow habits or on others building on you.
Outcome pricing
Charging for each successful result, such as a resolved ticket, rather than for seats or usage. Needs an agreed way to measure success.
AARRR
Five stages of growth: acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue. Each stage gets one event you can count.
Activation moment
The first time a new user gets the value your product promises.
Time-to-value
How long a new user takes to reach the activation moment, measured from sign-up.
Growth loop
A cycle where one user’s actions bring in the next user, so the output feeds back into the input.
Network effect
When a product gets better for existing users as more people use it. Different from virality, which only brings more people in.
Virality
Users bringing in other users, for example by sharing. It helps growth, but does not make the product better for anyone.
Dark pattern
A design that tricks users into acting against their own interest, such as a hidden cancel button or pre-ticked invitations.
Product-led growth
A go-to-market motion where users sign up and get value on their own, and some upgrade to paid, without talking to sales.
Input metric
A number the team can move directly, which you expect to move the North Star metric.
Event taxonomy
The list of events a product logs, with a naming rule everyone follows, such as object_action.
Tracking plan
The shared document listing every event, its properties, when it fires and who owns it.
Funnel
The share of users who complete each step of a process in order. It shows where people drop off.
Cohort
A group of users who started in the same period. Retention tables follow each cohort over time.
Minimum detectable effect
The smallest change an experiment is designed to detect. It sets how many users the test needs.
Selection bias
When the people in your data differ from the people you want to learn about, such as hand-picked early users.
State machine
A workflow where code fixes every step and every transition. The failing step is always known.
Bounded agent
An agent that chooses its own steps, but only from a fixed tool list and within a step budget and approval rules.
Design partner
An early user who agrees to use an unfinished product and tell you what they find, with clear consent.
Changelog
A short public note of what changed in each release, why, and what users should do differently.
Role matrix
A grid of real job descriptions against the skills they ask for, used to find the skills the market wants and your gaps.
A/B test
Showing two versions to two random groups of users at the same time and comparing one number between them, so you can tell which version caused the difference.
